children.text: A water submeter is a meter installed downstream of a property's main water meter to measure consumption for a smaller area, such as one apartment, condominium unit, commercial tenant, amenity space, irrigation system, or mechanical plant. The utility continues to read the main meter for the whole property; the submeters provide the unit-level detail that the main meter cannot.

For property owners and managers, that additional detail can support usage reporting, conservation, leak investigation, cost allocation, and tenant billing when the arrangement is permitted by the applicable rules. A complete
water submetering system
may also include remote-reading equipment, software, billing workflows, and dedicated leak sensors.
How Does a Water Submeter Work?

A water submeter records the volume of water passing through a particular pipe. Depending on the meter and system design, staff can read the register manually or collect the data through a pulse output, wired network, radio transmitter, cellular gateway, or another compatible communications method.

The difference between two validated readings represents consumption for the period. Before that usage is reported or billed, the system should confirm the measurement unit, meter multiplier, reading dates, unit assignment, and whether the reading passed the project's validation rules.
Main Water Meter Versus Water Submeter

The main meter is normally owned or controlled by the water utility and measures total water delivered to the property. A submeter is located after the main meter and measures only the branch it serves. Adding submeters does not automatically replace the utility's main meter, change the utility account, or create permission to bill occupants.

Submeter totals may not exactly equal the main-meter total. Timing differences, common-area consumption, irrigation, make-up water, meter tolerances, leaks, and unmetered branches can all create differences. A well-designed system identifies those sources instead of assuming every difference is a billing error.
Where Are Water Submeters Used?

Water submeters are commonly considered for multifamily apartments, condominiums, student housing, manufactured-home communities, mixed-use buildings, commercial tenants, office properties, retail spaces, and campuses. They can also measure shared loads such as cooling towers, boilers, laundry rooms, pools, irrigation, or other equipment.

The building's piping determines what can be measured. If one unit has a dedicated cold-water branch, unit-level metering may be straightforward. If several units share risers or a unit is supplied from multiple branches, the project may require multiple meters per unit, piping changes, or a different measurement strategy.
What Is Included in a Water Submetering System?
The meter is only one part of a dependable system. A typical project can include:
Water meters selected for the pipe size, expected flow range, water conditions, orientation, and intended use.
Pulse modules or digital outputs that make readings available to other equipment.
Transmitters, repeaters, gateways, wiring, or cellular communications.
Software for meter inventory, readings, validation, alerts, reporting, and billing files.
Dedicated
leak and flood sensors
for selected high-risk locations.
Commissioning records that connect each meter identifier to the correct unit or load.
Procedures for maintenance, estimated readings, corrections, vacancies, move-ins, move-outs, and resident questions.
What Are the Benefits of Water Submetering?
More Specific Consumption Information

A master bill shows the property's total. Submeters show where water is being used. Property teams can compare units, common areas, and equipment, investigate unexpected changes, and prioritize maintenance using more specific information.
Usage-Based Billing When Permitted

Where local rules and lease terms permit it, submeter readings can support charges based on measured consumption instead of estimates or allocation formulas. Transparent statements should show the billing period, readings, usage, rates, fees, adjustments, and a way to ask questions.
Earlier Investigation of Abnormal Usage

Continuous flow or an unexpected increase may point to a running toilet, dripping fixture, open valve, leak, incorrect unit assignment, or a change in occupancy. Meter data can help identify an anomaly, but it is not a substitute for dedicated leak sensors, inspections, or emergency response.
Accountability and Conservation

Unit-level reporting makes consumption visible to property teams and occupants. The actual effect depends on the building, fixtures, residents, pricing, communication, and maintenance practices, so savings should be measured rather than guaranteed.
How Are Water Submeters Installed?

A project should begin with a field survey. The survey documents the main service, pipe sizes, branches, unit layouts, shared loads, water temperature, expected flow, access, shutoffs, available space, communications conditions, and the purpose of the data.

After design and approvals, qualified trades coordinate shutdowns and install the meters according to manufacturer instructions and applicable plumbing requirements. Commissioning should verify flow direction, meter size, units, identifiers, communications, starting readings, and the connection between each physical meter and the correct account.

Existing buildings can often be retrofitted, but feasibility varies. Hidden or shared piping, finished ceilings, limited shutdown access, multiple feeds to one unit, or inadequate installation space can change the design and cost.
Can Water Submeters Be Read Remotely?

Many meters can be connected to remote-reading systems. The right approach depends on the number of meters, building construction, distance, power, available network, cybersecurity requirements, reading frequency, and long-term support.

A wireless label by itself does not guarantee reliable coverage. The design should account for concrete, mechanical rooms, shafts, metal enclosures, below-grade locations, radio congestion, battery replacement, and how missed readings will be recovered.
Can a Landlord Bill Tenants for Submetered Water?

Rules differ by province, state, municipality, property type, and how the readings will be used. Requirements may address meter approval, plumbing permits, lease disclosures, billing calculations, allowable fees, common-area usage, record retention, testing, disputes, shutoffs, and resident protections.

A property owner should not assume that installing a meter automatically permits tenant billing. The intended billing model should be reviewed before equipment is purchased or installed. Axis supports project assessment and operational planning, but property owners should obtain qualified local legal advice when necessary.
Water Submetering in Canada and the United States

Canada and the United States do not use one universal water-submetering rule. Canadian requirements can vary by province, municipality, utility, building type, and intended billing use. In the United States, state and local rules can differ substantially, including requirements for new construction, existing buildings, meter acceptance, disclosures, and resident billing.

For that reason, product and service claims should be tied to a defined jurisdiction and application. A meter suitable for internal monitoring may not automatically be accepted for occupant billing in every location.
How Much Does Water Submetering Cost?

There is no responsible single price without a property assessment. Project cost depends on unit count, number of meters per unit, pipe sizes, meter technology, installation access, plumbing changes, communications, gateways, leak sensors, commissioning, software, reading frequency, billing services, and ongoing maintenance.

When comparing proposals, property owners should look beyond the meter price. Confirm what is included for survey, design, installation, permits, commissioning, communications, data validation, warranty, maintenance, resident support, replacements, and billing.
Questions to Ask a Water Submetering Provider
Has the building's piping and unit layout been verified in the field?
How were meter size, minimum flow, maximum flow, and installation orientation selected?
Which approvals or reviews apply to the intended use of the readings?
How are meter identifiers and unit assignments commissioned and audited?
What happens when a reading is missing, duplicated, reversed, or unusually high?
How are common-area and vacant-unit consumption handled?
Who maintains meters, transmitters, gateways, batteries, and software?
What information will residents see, and how are billing questions resolved?
Next Step for Property Owners

A successful water-submetering project connects suitable equipment, qualified installation, verified data, transparent billing, and ongoing support. If you are evaluating a new development, occupied-building retrofit, or an existing system that needs replacement, review Axis's
water submetering services
or
request a property assessment
